Research / Educational Case Study · Learning Report

Financial Statement Study · Industrials

Working Capital Cycles and ROCE Decomposition in Indian Manufacturing

How to decompose Return on Capital Employed (ROCE) into asset turnover and operating margin, and how inventory and receivable days impact cash flow in capital-intensive businesses.

  • Document ClassificationEducational case study / learning report (mentor-reviewed)
  • AuthorHarion Research Learning Lab (Mentor-Reviewed Sample)
  • Published Date2026-09-28
  • Positions DisclosedNo position disclosed. Prepared strictly as an educational template.
Educational Notice: This report is prepared solely as an academic and analytical case study demonstrating financial research methodology. It contains no target price, no buy/sell/hold rating, and is not investment advice.

1. DuPont decomposition on reported filings

Two manufacturing companies can report the exact same 18% Return on Capital Employed (ROCE) through completely different economic models. One may operate with high gross margins and slow asset turnover (specialized industrial equipment), while another operates on thin margins with rapid inventory turnover (consumables and light engineering). Separating EBIT margin from capital-employed turnover is the first step in financial modelling.

2. Reading the cash conversion cycle

Reported net profit on the income statement does not pay for capacity expansion; cash flow from operations does. By calculating Inventory Days, Trade Receivable Days, and Trade Payable Days across 5 years of annual reports, interns learn to spot whether revenue growth is accompanied by healthy cash collection or by stretching channel credit.

3. Combining fundamental and price-structure lenses

In the Market Analysis Learning Lab, learners observe how multi-year changes in balance-sheet debt and capital work-in-progress (CWIP) interact with long-term market structure. When new plant capacity is commissioned, depreciation and interest expenses rise immediately while utilization ramps gradually—an accounting dynamic that purely price-based or purely single-period ratio screens can miss if studied in isolation.

4. Limitations & verification checklist

Consolidated vs. standalone statements, accounting policy changes in inventory valuation (FIFO vs. weighted average), and related-party transactions require reading the Notes to Accounts in the full annual report. Screeners help narrow a universe of stocks; primary filings provide the context.
